{{Orphan|date=December 2019}}

'''Newest Vertex Bisection''' is an [[algorithm]]ic method to locally refine [[triangulation]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Convergence and quasi-optimality of adaptive FEM with inhomogeneous Dirichlet data |journal = Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics|volume = 255|issue = 100|last=Feischl |first=M. |last2=Page |first2=M. |date=2014-01-01 |pages=481–501 |doi=10.1016/j.cam.2013.06.009 |pmc=3798050 |pmid=24391306 |last3=Praetorius |first3=D.}}</ref> It is widely used in [[computational science]], [[numerical simulation]], and [[computer graphics]]. The advantage of newest vertex bisection is that it allows local refinement of triangulations without degenerating the shape of the triangles after repeated usage.<ref>Mitchell, William F. "30 years of newest vertex bisection." AIP Conference Proceedings. Vol. 1738. No. 1. AIP Publishing, 2016.</ref>

In newest vertex bisection, whenever a triangle is to be split into smaller triangles, it will be bisected by drawing a line from the newest [[Vertex (geometry)|vertex]] to the midpoint of the edge opposite to that vertex. That midpoint becomes the newest vertex of the two newer triangles. One can show that repeating this procedure for a given triangulation leads to triangles that belong to only a finite number of [[similarity (geometry)|similarity classes]].

Generalizations of newest vertex bisection to dimension three and higher are known.<ref>Maubach, Joseph M. "Local bisection refinement for n-simplicial grids generated by reflection." SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 16.1 (1995): 210–227.</ref> Newest vertex bisection is used in local mesh refinement for adaptive [[finite element method]]s,<ref>Arnold, Douglas N., Arup Mukherjee, and Luc Pouly. "Locally adapted tetrahedral meshes using bisection." SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 22.2 (2000): 431–448.</ref> where it is an alternative to [[red-green refinement]] and [[uniform mesh refinement]].
